newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ritz-Carlton tries to woo Japanese amid hotel glut.
newsitem.headline: Ritz-Carlton tries to woo Japanese amid hotel glut.

text.p: The Ritz-Carlton has arrived in Japan's western capital to lure more Japanese guests -- but industry sources say Osakans, spoiled by a hotel glut, will prove tough customers for the U.S. luxury chain.

"The Japanese are our most important customer outside the U.S.," Horst Schulze, president and chief executive officer of the Ritz-Carlton, told Reuters in an interview. "Over 35 percent of our business in Asia comes from Japan, so we must be in Japan to secure our outbound customers."

The Ritz, which is 49 percent owned by Host Mariott Corp and operates 33 hotels worldwide, last week opened a flagship hotel in western Japan's biggest city and the nation's traditional commercial centre.

The Ritz's luxury rooms, furnished with 19th century European antiques, cost 27,000 yen ($232) a night, not a shocking amount for Osaka locals who are used to spending money on western fashion brands such as Chanel and Armani.
A night in one of its suites -- yours for a mere 450,000 yen ($3,879) per night -- could be their dream come true.
But industry analysts said the Ritz will not be immune to competition amid a glut of luxury hotels here, especially if they keep their prices high.

"Business-oriented hotels in the city don't stand much of a chance," said Tsuyoshi Taniguchi, an analyst at Nikko Research Centre. "Hotels across Japan are trying to maintain relatively high occupancy rates by suppressing prices," he added.
Osaka is host to a range of prestigious hotels including the Imperial Hotel, The New Otani, The Westin and The Hilton, owned by Hilton Hotels Corp.

Industry sources said the opening of the Kansai International Airport in 1994 prompted some to enter the Osaka market, and now hopes for the city's mega-projects such as the Universal Studios, due to open here in 2001, have lured more.
Osaka's bid for the Olympic Games in 2008 is also an incentive, they said.
But the hotel gold rush is forcing some to slash prices.
One of the Japan's classiest hotels, The Imperial, broke from its snobbish image and opened an Osaka branch last year with a 50 percent discount throughout the first half year.
On possible competition from the Ritz, Imperial's Marketing Manager Saeko Yamanaka said: "The Ritz's price of 35,000 yen ($301) for a twin room is close to the upper limit. We are not that worried."
ANA Hotel Osaka, linked with All Nippon Airways Co Ltd, was also forced to offer a discount of 3,000 yen ($25) per room this April, the first time they did so since opening in 1984.
A spokeswoman for the ANA Hotel said the occupancy rate climbed to 80 percent from around 70 after the price cut.

"The Ritz always says they hope to secure the top five percent of executive business travellers in every city they have branches, but I doubt how much of that market is present in Osaka," one manager at a major hotel in Osaka said.
Industry sources said the Westin Osaka, which opened in 1993, is facing tough times due to its reluctance to bring prices down.

"The bottom line is still prices. Room charges are still relatively high in Japan and with the economy stagnating, demand from corporate customers cannot be expected to pick up soon," said Nikko's Taniguchi.
